What happens to a whale after it dies?
Picture a creature weighing up
to two hundred tons,
taking its very last breath in
the open ocean.
The answer reveals one of the most
astonishing, beautiful, and alien
phenomena in all of natural science.
And it begins with a long,
silent fall into the dark.
When a whale dies,
its journey does not simply come
to a quiet end.
An adult whale carries tens of
thousands of kilograms of rich
organic matter: blubber, muscle,
organs, and a skeleton packed with fat.
In the natural world,
death is rarely a void.
It is a catalyst for radical transformation.
And what follows the death of a
single whale can feed communities
of deep-sea animals for decades.
Scientists did not even know this
world existed until 1987.
That year, researchers diving in
the submersible Alvin, in the Santa
Catalina Basin off California,
came across the skeleton of a gray
whale resting on the seafloor,
swarming with strange life.
It was the first whale fall
community that scientists studied up close.
Since then, researchers have studied
whale falls by finding them with
robotic submarines and by revisiting
them again and again over the years.
The real miracle happens when the
carcass does not wash up on a
beach, but sinks into the open sea.
Marine biologists call this a whale fall.
Many carcasses float for a while,
buoyed by the gases of decomposition.
Once those gases escape,
or if the whale was lean and
dense to begin with,
the body sinks.
Slowly, the carcass begins a silent
descent, traveling thousands of
meters down into perpetual darkness.
To understand a whale fall,
you must understand the deep seafloor.
The abyssal plains cover a huge
share of our planet,
and much of that ground is a
biological desert.
Sunlight never reaches it,
temperatures hover near freezing,
and the pressure is crushing.
Food is scarce.
Most animals live on marine snow,
which is tiny flakes of dead
plankton and debris drifting down from above.
For this starved world,
a whale is a windfall beyond comprehension.
After hours or even days of falling,
the whale touches down on the muddy plain.
The impact likely kicks up thick
clouds of silt.
In an instant, a flat,
barren landscape has gained a
mountain of food.
Scientists divide the life of a
whale fall into four overlapping
stages, and the first begins right
away: the mobile-scavenger stage.
Although the deep ocean seems empty,
news travels fast through chemical currents.
Scent trails from the carcass spread
through the cold water,
and scavengers with highly sensitive
chemical senses can pick them up
from far away.
One by one, they begin swimming
against the current toward the source.
A banquet has just been delivered
to a seafloor that has gone hungry
for a very long time.
Among the first big visitors are sharks.
Pacific sleeper sharks have been
filmed feeding on whale carcasses
on the seafloor.
These sluggish, ancient-looking
predators bite into thick blubber
and shake their bodies to tear
off chunks of flesh.
Because the food is so abundant,
animals that usually hunt alone
can end up sharing the same meal.
Joining the sharks are hagfish,
primitive jawless fish from a
lineage that has lasted hundreds
of millions of years.
With no true jaws,
they rasp flesh away with toothlike
plates made of keratin.
Hagfish can burrow right into a
carcass and eat it from the inside out.
And when threatened, they release
huge amounts of slime,
one of the strangest defenses in
the animal kingdom.
Then come the crustaceans.
Giant isopods, armored cousins
of the pill bugs in your garden,
can grow longer than thirty
centimeters and are known for
swarming carcasses on the deep seafloor.
They can survive long stretches
without food, so when a feast
finally arrives, they make the most of it.
Together with swarms of smaller
scavenging crustaceans, they can
cover a carcass in a shifting carpet
of armor and legs.
This stage is astonishingly fast,
even in the cold and the dark.
Researchers estimate that scavengers
can strip forty to sixty kilograms
of soft tissue from a carcass every
single day.
Within several months to about
two years, the flesh,
blubber, and organs of one of the
largest animals on Earth are gone.
What remains is a bare skeleton
resting on the sea floor.
But the story is only just beginning.
With the big scavengers gone,
the whale fall enters its second
phase, the opportunistic stage,
which lasts for months to a few years.
The target now is not big chunks
of meat, but the scraps scattered
across the surrounding mud.
During the feeding frenzy,
huge amounts of tissue,
fat, and organic dust sank into the sediment.
This creates a nutrient-rich halo
around the skeleton that reaches
several meters outward.
Worms, crustaceans, and small
mollusks now arrive in huge numbers
to colonize the enriched mud.
Bristle worms called polychaetes
burrow through the sediment,
feeding on the bacteria that thrive
on whale fat.
Small snails and limpets graze
on the greasy bone.
Their numbers can climb far above
those of the surrounding seabed,
making a whale fall one of the
busiest places in the deep ocean.
But the real prize remains locked
inside the skeleton.
Whale bones are porous and
spongelike, and inside them lies
a huge reservoir of fats.
By some estimates, these lipids
can make up as much as about
six percent of the whale's original
body weight.
The fats are sealed inside the
bone, out of reach of ordinary scavengers.
Unlocking this hidden vault takes
a very different kind of life.
This brings us to the third and
most chemically miraculous stage,
the sulfophilic, or sulfur-loving stage.
It can last for decades,
with estimates reaching eighty
years or more for the largest
whales, which makes it the longest
chapter of a whale fall.
Deep inside the bone,
bacteria that live without oxygen
break down the fats using sulfate
dissolved in seawater.
Their waste product is hydrogen
sulfide, a toxic gas.
For most animals, hydrogen sulfide
is a poison.
But on the abyssal plain, it is fuel.
Chemosynthetic bacteria coat the
skeleton in thick, pale mats,
using the sulfide to make energy
without a single drop of sunlight.
This turns a dead whale into an
ecosystem similar to deep-sea
hydrothermal vents and cold seeps,
a tiny chemical oasis in the middle
of a barren desert.
On the surface of our planet,
almost all life runs on sunlight.
Plants and algae capture it,
and animals eat them.
Chemosynthesis flips that story.
Instead of sunlight, these bacteria
use the energy stored in chemicals,
like hydrogen sulfide.
Animals that cannot make their
own food simply partner with the
bacteria, giving them shelter in
exchange for a steady supply of energy.
Living among these bacteria is
one of the most bizarre animals
ever discovered: Osedax, nicknamed
the zombie worm, or the bone-eating worm.
Researchers first found it in 2002,
on a gray whale skeleton in Monterey
Canyon, off California.
These worms have no mouth and no stomach.
Instead, they have bright red,
feathery plumes that take in oxygen
from the cold seawater.
Anchored to the skeleton,
they look like crimson flowers
blooming across a graveyard of bones.
How can a creature without a mouth
feed on solid bone?
The secret is its roots.
The lower part of the female Osedax
grows into the bone and releases
acid that dissolves it.
Inside those root-like tissues
live symbiotic bacteria that break
down the collagen and fats in the
bone, and the worm absorbs the nutrients.
In a very real sense,
these worms melt their way into
the skeleton to reach food that
has been locked away inside.
The reproductive life of Osedax
is even stranger.
Every visible, feathery worm is female.
So where are the males?
They are microscopic dwarves,
far smaller than their mates,
living inside the female's
gelatinous tube, sometimes dozens
in a single tube.
They do not feed on bone.
They exist to fertilize her eggs,
so that larvae can drift out on
the ocean currents in search of
the next fallen giant.
Since that first discovery,
researchers have found many
different species of Osedax,
living on whale bones in oceans
around the world.
Their larvae seem to find bones
from far away, though how they
do it is still being studied.
Wherever a whale skeleton rests
on the seafloor, there may be a
field of these tiny red flowers
waiting for it.
Alongside the zombie worms,
clusters of mussels, clams,
and limpets settle on the bones.
These animals do not filter plankton
like their shallow-water cousins.
Instead, their gills host bacteria
that use the hydrogen sulfide
seeping from the bones.
In this pitch-black graveyard,
life runs on chemistry.
A whole web of animals can flourish
on the cold bones,
decades after the whale took its last breath.
Some biologists think whale falls
play another role: stepping stones.
Hydrothermal vents can be separated
by hundreds or even thousands of
kilometers of barren seafloor,
and many vent animals struggle
to cross such distances as larvae.
One hypothesis is that whale falls,
scattered across the deep sea,
offer resting spots along the way,
helping vent animals spread across
ocean basins over millions of years.
The idea is still debated.
Decades pass.
Eventually, the fats and sulfur
compounds in the skeleton run out.
The bacteria and worms,
starved of fuel, slowly die off.
Yet the whale fall still shapes
the deep sea, through what
scientists call the reef stage.
Even after the last nourishment
has been used up,
the bare mineral skeleton remains
on the muddy seafloor.
On the abyssal plains,
hard surfaces are rare.
The ground is mostly soft mud and silt.
Animals that need something solid
to hold on to,
such as corals, sponges,
anemones, and crinoids, have very
few places to settle.
A whale skull or rib cage can
become one of them,
a small natural reef where filter
feeders attach and lift themselves
above the mud.
Mobile animals may use the ruins too.
Fish and other creatures can shelter
among the ribs and vertebrae,
using the bones as a hiding place
in a world with almost no landscape.
How long the reef stage lasts is
hard to say.
Over a very long time,
seawater and currents slowly
dissolve the bone, and the skeleton
fades into the sediment,
returning its minerals to the seafloor.
Let us put the four stages side by side.
The scavengers feast for months,
up to about two years.
The opportunists follow for months
to a few years.
The sulfur lovers can last for decades.
And the reef stage lasts for as
long as the bones endure,
which no one knows exactly.
Whale falls may also matter for the climate.
A whale collects a great deal of
carbon in its body over a life
that can last many decades.
When it sinks to the deep seafloor,
that carbon is carried far from
the surface and can stay buried
in the deep for a very long time.
Scientists call this natural
conveyor the biological carbon
pump, and whales are one small part of it.
But this ancient system was disrupted.
Industrial whaling in the twentieth
century killed an estimated 2.9
million great whales, according
to a 2014 study by Rocha and colleagues.
Whales processed on ships or on
land never sank to the seafloor,
so the deep lost its feasts.
Some scientists suspect that whaling
removed a large share of natural
whale falls, though the exact number
is uncertain.
For animals that depend on whale
falls, this may have been devastating.
There is a hopeful note, however.
Commercial whaling was put on hold
by a global moratorium that began
in 1986, and some whale populations
have been slowly recovering since.
As their numbers grow,
more whales will die naturally
and sink, and the deep seafloor
may slowly see more of these ancient
feasts return.
There is a hauntingly poetic idea
woven into the story of a whale fall.
In our world, death is often seen
as an ending, marked by loss and silence.
Yet in the deep,
cold ocean, the death of a single
creature breathes life into a whole
community of animals.
One majestic life gives up its
form, so that many unseen,
wondrous creatures can thrive in
an otherwise frozen desert.
As you look across the calm surface
of the ocean today,
remember the secret hidden beneath it.
Somewhere right now, thousands
of meters below the rocking swells,
the skeleton of a fallen giant
is quietly feeding an oasis of life.
It is a reminder that even in
the darkest, coldest corners of
our world, life finds a way.
A single death in the open ocean
becomes a home for countless living things.
What other quiet wonders are hiding
beneath the waves, still waiting
for someone to notice?
